accuracy.evidence: Checked against English Appendix 2 of the national curriculum (Year 3 terminology: clause, subordinate clause, conjunction, preposition; Year 2 co-ordination with or, and, but and subordination with when, if, that, because) and its glossary definitions of clause, main clause and subordinate clause, plus Common Core L.3.1h, L.3.1i and L.4.1f. The flip test is a standard classroom check: only the subordinate clause can be fronted, with a comma.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the known slips: writing a subordinate clause alone as a sentence (the fragment step and the challenge item 'Although it was late.'), assuming the first clause is the main one (main-clause sentence 2 and challenge tag 'first'), treating a noun phrase as a clause (tag 'noun'), and calling after or until a conjunction before a phrase (the preposition step).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagclause is about grammatical status, not meaning: it tests verb or no verb, stand-alone or dependent, and whether a clause can move. flagwhen (Expressing Time, Place and Cause) sorts when, where and why meanings and flagfront places commas after adverbials; neither classifies conjunctions as coordinating or subordinating or mends fragments. The shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each term comes from a test the child runs: tapping a non-verb in 'after lunch' explains there is no action, lifting 'because it rained' out shows it ending in '…?' with a dashed underline, and the Flip it button shows 'Because he wanted to read, Sam stayed up late.' marked as still making sense while 'So we took our coats, it was raining.' is marked as not working.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'Yes, it has a verb' for whether 'because it rained' can stand alone, 'but he felt fine' as the clause that can move to the front, and 'A conjunction' for after in 'We played after lunch'. Each is tested by the task that follows, and the done message reveals the child's own choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with ten tagged wrong answers, each with its own correction: phrase vs clause, noun phrase with no verb, 'Coming first does not make it main', because and when passing the flip test, 'A verb, came, follows until, so it starts a clause', until is not an action, and a lone subordinate clause needing a main clause.

readability.evidence: Learner text stays under the learner kid limit of 6.5 with short sentences ('That is a main clause. Other clauses leave you waiting.'), and the adult text stays under 9.5 while naming English Appendix 2, the Year 2 and Year 3 terms and CCSS L.3.1h, L.3.1i and L.4.1f. The exact terms main clause, subordinate clause, coordinating and subordinating conjunction and preposition are used throughout.

no_filler.evidence: The filler gate passed. Kid paragraphs each teach one test with an example sentence; adult paragraphs give the standards, the three tests, the named mistakes and the lab outline. Overlap with Expressing Time, Place and Cause, Joining Words with And and Fronted Adverbials is under the 12 percent limit.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360x640 in light and dark show word cards in centred rows, long sentence cards capped to the canvas width with readable text, and the Coordinating and Subordinating targets as two large boxes. Every canvas card also has a button below the canvas; phone_sweep reported 0 findings.

accessibility.evidence: axe reported no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark on desktop and iPhone 13, with no console errors. All canvas text uses the theme text colour on the panel colour. Every tap target has a labelled button twin (the words, the clauses, the fragment endings, Flip it, the two conjunction kinds, Conjunction and Preposition), and the canvas aria-label speaks each result.
